newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Geneva raises landing fees for Swissair.
newsitem.headline: Geneva raises landing fees for Swissair.

text.p: Geneva's Cointrin Airport plans to lower landing fees by 10 percent in general, but double the fees charged for domestic flights -- a direct blow to Swissair AG, the Swiss national carrier said on Wednesday.
The move by Geneva's airport, owned by the canton of Geneva, is the latest sign of Geneva's anger over Swissair's decision in April to scrap 13 of 15 intercontinental flights from Geneva.
"Geneva Airport's intention to double the landing fees for domestic flights is seen by Swissair as a blow against Swiss airlines," Swissair said in a statement.
Air transport in Switzerland is dominated by Swissair and its regional airline subsidiary Crossair AG.
Swissair said the doubling in landing fees would add another 1.2 million Swiss francs to the cost of running its already loss-making flights between Zurich and Geneva.
It said the airport authorities in Geneva today made public its proposal to change the fee structure.
"The Swissair Group as the main customer of Geneva airport expects a general reduction in tariffs instead of a targeted, massive increase for Swiss companies," Swissair said.

Swissair's decision to concentrate its long-haul flights in its Zurich hub and withdraw some direct intercontinental flights from Geneva caused an outcry in Geneva, the capital of the French-speaking region of Switzerland.
Many Swiss politicians criticised Swissair's move as a threat to national unity and it also reignited smoldering tensions between the French and German-speaking parts of the Alpine country.
Although Swissair acknowledged its obligations as a national carrier, it said the decision was vital for its future.
In response to the bitter criticism, Swissair said it would improve services between Geneva and Zurich with shuttle flights that will connect the two cities 10 times daily.
The new shuttle service will begin end-October.

The Swiss government has said it would lift Swissair's monopoly status and in June the city of Geneva decided to sell its 19,000 shares in Swissair -- 0.8 percent of the carrier's share capital -- to protest the move.
